title: Claude vs ChatGPT: Which AI Assistant Should You Choose?
excerpt: Claude and ChatGPT both handle writing and coding well — here's how to pick based on your actual workflow, not hype.
content:
Claude and ChatGPT are the two AI assistants most people compare first, and for good reason: both handle general conversation, writing, and coding well enough that the choice often comes down to workflow fit rather than raw capability.

## Where Claude tends to win

Claude has built a reputation around long-form writing and editing. Feed it a messy draft and it tends to preserve your voice rather than flattening it into generic AI-speak — useful for anyone who writes for a living or just doesn't want their emails to sound like everyone else's ChatGPT output. It's also become a favorite for agentic, multi-step coding work: tasks that involve reading across an existing codebase, making coordinated edits, and iterating based on test results rather than answering a single isolated question. And when you need to work through a long document — a contract, a research paper, a large codebase file — Claude's handling of long context tends to stay coherent rather than losing track of earlier details.

## Where ChatGPT tends to win

ChatGPT's biggest advantage is breadth. It's the default most people already have installed, it has the largest plugin and integration ecosystem, and its multimodal features (image generation via DALL·E, voice mode, and browsing) are all bundled into one place. If you want a single tool that can also generate an image, search the web, and hold a voice conversation without switching apps, ChatGPT's ecosystem is hard to beat. It also tends to have a slight edge for very short, quick-turnaround tasks where you just want a fast answer without much back-and-forth.

## The honest answer

Neither tool is strictly "better" — they're optimized for different habits. If most of your work is writing, editing, or coding on real projects, Claude's steadiness over long tasks is worth trying. If you want one app that does a bit of everything — chat, image generation, voice, search — ChatGPT's breadth is the more convenient default.

A lot of people who use AI tools daily end up with both: one for serious writing and coding work, the other for quick everyday questions. Given both offer usable free tiers, the cheapest way to find out which fits your workflow is to actually run the same real task through both for a week.

title: Midjourney vs DALL·E 3 vs Stable Diffusion: Picking the Right AI Image Generator
excerpt: These three tools solve different problems. Here's how to choose based on style, control, and cost.
content:
Ask ten people which AI image generator is "best" and you'll get ten different answers — because Midjourney, DALL·E 3, and Stable Diffusion aren't really solving the same problem. Here's how to actually pick between them.

## Midjourney — for a distinctive look

Midjourney has a house style: painterly, atmospheric, and immediately recognizable even without a watermark. It's the go-to for concept art, mood boards, and marketing visuals where you want something that looks intentionally designed rather than photorealistic. The trade-off is control — Midjourney's prompt syntax takes practice, and getting exact text or precise composition right is harder than with some competitors. If your goal is "make this look striking," Midjourney is usually the fastest path there.

## DALL·E 3 — for following instructions precisely

DALL·E 3's strength is doing exactly what you asked. Because it's built on top of a language model (accessible directly through ChatGPT), you can describe a scene in plain, detailed English — including specific text you want rendered — and it tends to follow the brief closely rather than reinterpreting it artistically. That makes it a strong choice for illustrating blog posts, social content, or anything where you already know exactly what you want and just need it rendered accurately. It's also the most convenient option if you're already inside a ChatGPT conversation and want to iterate on an image without switching tools.

## Stable Diffusion — for control and cost at scale

Stable Diffusion is open-source and self-hostable, which changes the economics entirely: once you're set up, there's no per-image API cost, which matters if you're generating images by the thousands. It's also the only one of the three you can fine-tune on your own style, brand, or dataset — useful for teams that need consistent, on-brand output rather than a one-off image. The trade-off is setup complexity: getting good results requires more technical investment than typing a prompt into a web app.

## Quick picks by use case

- **Concept art, mood boards, striking visuals** → Midjourney
- **Precise, instruction-following images, especially with text** → DALL·E 3
- **High-volume generation, custom fine-tuning, no per-image cost** → Stable Diffusion

Most serious creative workflows end up using more than one — Midjourney for the initial look, DALL·E 3 for quick precise edits, Stable Diffusion when volume or customization matters.

title: GitHub Copilot vs Cursor: Which AI Coding Tool Is Right for You?
excerpt: Extension vs. full editor, agent capability, pricing, and model flexibility — compared for 2026.
content:
GitHub Copilot and Cursor both went from "autocomplete with extra steps" to genuinely agentic coding tools over the past year, and the comparison in 2026 looks pretty different than it did when Cursor first launched.

## The core difference: extension vs. editor

Copilot is an extension that plugs into editors you already use — VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, and others — layering AI on top of your existing setup. Cursor is a full editor in its own right, a VS Code fork rebuilt from the ground up around AI-first workflows. That architectural choice shapes everything else: Copilot prioritizes low friction and staying inside your current tools, while Cursor asks you to switch editors in exchange for deeper, more integrated AI capability.

## Agent capability

Both ship real agent modes now. Copilot's Agent Mode (which reached general availability in IDEs like VS Code and JetBrains in March 2026) can create branches, edit across multiple files, run tests, and open pull requests autonomously — and it plugs directly into GitHub Actions and your existing CI/CD setup. Cursor's Composer-driven agent works similarly inside the editor, and its Background Agents feature (available on higher tiers) can run multiple parallel coding sessions on cloud VMs using separate git worktrees — useful if you want several tasks progressing at once rather than one at a time.

On independent coding benchmarks, the two land close together — recent results put Copilot slightly ahead on raw task-solve rate, while Cursor tends to complete tasks faster. In practice, the gap is small enough that workflow fit matters more than the benchmark numbers.

## Model flexibility

Both support multiple frontier models (GPT, Claude, and Gemini variants) as of 2026, but the way you pick between them differs. Cursor leans into explicit per-task model selection — you can route cheaper tasks to a fast model and switch to a frontier model for harder reasoning. Copilot's model selection is available too, with GitHub's February 2026 update adding the ability to assign different models per issue, though it's generally less granular than Cursor's routing.

## Pricing and ecosystem

Copilot Pro runs about $10/month; Cursor Pro is roughly double that at $20/month, with higher Pro+/Ultra tiers for teams running Background Agents heavily. Copilot's other real advantage is ambient context: if your team already lives in GitHub, Copilot indexes your repo, PR history, and issues automatically — context Cursor can't replicate without extra setup.

## Which one should you pick?

- **Already deep in the GitHub ecosystem, want the cheaper option** → GitHub Copilot
- **Want the highest ceiling for large-codebase, multi-file agentic work, and don't mind switching editors** → Cursor
- **Not sure?** → A common pattern among developers is running both: Copilot for everyday coding inside your existing setup, Cursor for the heaviest refactors and multi-file work.

- [Cursor](/browse/tools/cursor)

title: Runway vs Synthesia: Choosing the Right AI Video Tool
excerpt: Generative creative video vs. reliable presenter-style video — these solve nearly opposite problems.
content:
Runway and Synthesia both make AI video tools, but they solve almost opposite problems — one is for creative, generative video work, the other for fast, repeatable presenter-style content.

## Runway — generative and creative

Runway is built around text-to-video generation and AI-assisted editing: describe a scene and generate original footage, or use its editing tools (inpainting, green-screen-style background removal, motion tracking) on existing clips. It's the pick for short-form creative content, motion graphics, and experimental visuals where you want something that doesn't look like stock footage. The trade-off is that generative video is still inherently a bit unpredictable — you'll often generate several takes before landing on the one that works, so it suits an iterative, exploratory workflow rather than a fixed production schedule.

## Synthesia — reliable and repeatable

Synthesia takes a completely different approach: AI avatars that present scripted content on camera, without ever filming a real person. That makes it the strongest option for training videos, e-learning modules, and product explainers — content types where you need to update the script regularly and don't want to re-film every time something changes. Its multilingual dubbing (translating the same video into dozens of languages with a matching avatar) is a genuine differentiator for companies localizing training or onboarding content across regions.

## Quick picks by use case

- **Creative, generative footage, short-form content, motion graphics** → Runway
- **Training videos, e-learning, explainer videos, multilingual localization** → Synthesia

If you're a content creator or agency doing creative work, Runway is the natural fit. If you're a company that regularly needs to produce or update instructional/presenter-style video without a production team, Synthesia will save far more time.

title: Intercom Fin vs Zendesk AI: Comparing AI Customer Support Tools
excerpt: AI-first ticket resolution vs. AI-assisted agents on an established platform — which fits your support stack?
content:
If you're choosing an AI layer for customer support, the decision usually comes down to one question: are you building a new support stack around AI, or adding AI to a support platform you already run?

## Intercom Fin — AI-first support

Fin is built as an AI-first support agent: it's trained directly on your help docs and past conversations, and it's designed to resolve common tickets end-to-end rather than just suggesting a reply for a human to approve. When it can't resolve something confidently, it escalates cleanly to a human agent with the conversation context intact. This makes it a strong fit for teams that want AI doing the front-line resolution work, with humans handling the exceptions.

## Zendesk AI — AI layered onto an established platform

Zendesk AI takes a more augmentative approach: AI-suggested replies for agents, automatic ticket triage and routing, and analytics that surface your most common issue types. Rather than replacing the human-in-the-loop model, it speeds up the agents you already have. If you're already running Zendesk for ticketing and just want to make your existing team faster, this is the lower-friction path — no need to migrate your support stack.

## Quick picks by use case

- **Want AI to autonomously resolve routine tickets, not just assist agents** → Intercom Fin
- **Already run Zendesk and want to speed up your existing agents rather than replace the workflow** → Zendesk AI

Both tools plug into the same broader trend — AI absorbing the repetitive front line of support so human agents spend their time on the harder, higher-context cases. The right pick mostly depends on whether you're building your support stack from scratch or improving one that's already working.

title: Recent Moves in AI Coding Tools: Copilot and Cursor Catch Up to Each Other
excerpt: Agent modes reached general availability on both sides this year, and pricing has diverged rather than converged.
content:
The AI coding tool category has moved fast this year, and if you haven't checked in on GitHub Copilot or Cursor since early 2026, quite a bit has changed on both sides.

## Agent modes are now table stakes

Both tools shipped fully autonomous agent modes that reached general availability this year. GitHub's Copilot Agent Mode — generally available in VS Code and JetBrains as of March 2026 — can now create branches, edit across multiple files, run tests, self-heal on failures, and open pull requests without step-by-step guidance, wired directly into GitHub Actions and existing CI/CD pipelines. Copilot's CLI also reached general availability in February 2026, extending that same agentic behavior to the terminal. Cursor's equivalent, Composer, works similarly inside its own editor, with a Background Agents feature that runs multiple parallel coding sessions on cloud VMs using separate git worktrees — useful for tackling several tasks at once instead of one at a time.

## Model choice has expanded on both sides

Both tools now support routing across multiple frontier models — GPT, Claude, and Gemini variants — rather than locking you into one provider. Cursor leans into granular, per-task model selection, letting you send cheap tasks to a fast model and harder reasoning to a frontier one. GitHub's February 2026 update added a comparable ability to assign different models per issue, closing some of the gap, though Cursor's routing is still generally considered more flexible.

## Pricing has diverged, not converged

GitHub Copilot Pro sits at roughly $10/month; Cursor Pro is about double that at $20/month, with Pro+ and Ultra tiers aimed at teams running Background Agents heavily. That's a genuine trade-off rather than one tool simply being "better value" — Copilot's price advantage comes with less granular agent tooling, while Cursor's higher price buys deeper codebase understanding and more agent flexibility.

## The takeaway

Independent benchmarks now put the two tools close together on raw coding task performance, with Copilot edging ahead on solve rate and Cursor completing tasks faster — close enough that the deciding factor for most teams is whether you're already deep in the GitHub ecosystem (favors Copilot) or want the highest ceiling for large, multi-file agentic work and don't mind switching editors (favors Cursor).
